chapter_theme: The means of perfecting the body (காயசித்தி உபாயம்): since the body is the ground of life and of true knowledge, and the Lord has made it his temple, it is to be nurtured, not despised; breath control, mantra, the raising of the vital airs, restraint of food and union with Shakti are given as the means by which the body is cleansed, made young and kept from death.
structure_note: Two opening verses in the first person state the turn from despising the body to cherishing it (724, 725). The rest gives the means: cleansing by breath and the humours (726, 727), a set of yogic diagrams and counts (728, 729), inner sound, mantra and the raising of prana and apana (730 to 733), Shakti and the reversal of age (734 to 736), and the defeat of Death (737 to 739). Several verses close with an oath on Nandi (ஆணையே).

724.reading: If the body perishes, the life perishes, and one cannot firmly attain true knowledge; so, having learned the means of nurturing the body, I nurtured the body and with it nurtured life.
724.nuance: The argument is practical: the body is kept because knowledge (மெய்ஞ்ஞானம்) needs time and a living frame to be won. உபாயம் is left unnamed here; the chapter supplies it.

725.reading: I once held the body to be a thing of shame; then within the body I saw the true substance, and knowing that the Highest has made the body his temple, I now cherish it.
725.nuance: The verse narrates a change of mind: இழுக்கு (a fault, something base) is the view Tirumular says he held first, the ascetic contempt for the body. உத்தமன் கோயில் கொண்டான் makes the body a temple, and ஓம்புதல் is the word for caring for something precious.

726.reading: Turning the breath round cleanses and drives out; for those who know the means of loosening the impurity, filling the lotus and circulating it, the heat ceases and the body becomes like collyrium.
726.nuance: Breath is not named; சுழற்றி (whirling) and கமலத்துப் பூரித்து (filling at the lotus) are traditionally taken as the inhalation (puraka) and circulation of breath. மலம் here may be bodily waste or the soul's impurity. அஞ்சனம் (black eye-salve) is unclear as an image: a dark, lustrous, unaging body is one reading, an invisible one (the salve of the magicians) another. The variant சுழித்து changes little.

727.reading: With the body like collyrium, practice in the evening removes phlegm, at midday the treacherous wind, and in the early morning bile; we have spoken so that the poison goes, and grey hair and wrinkles are destroyed.
727.nuance: ஐ, வாதம் and பித்தம் are the three humours of Tamil medicine (kapha, vata, pitta), each matched to a time of day. What is to be done at those times (செய்திடில்) is not named; the chapter suggests breath practice. நரைதிரை (greying and wrinkling) are the marks of age the chapter promises to undo, as again in 734.

728.reading: The serpents of three coils, the two and the eight, the yantra that holds, the twelve finger-breadths, and the two hanging eggs tied there: whoever stays fixed so will not lose the body.
728.nuance: Almost every term is technical. The coiled serpent is traditionally kundalini, twelve finger-breadths the measure of the breath, and the two hanging eggs (முட்டை இரண்டு) are taken by some as the testes, tied in a yogic lock; பாம்பு இரண்டு எட்டு may be nadis or the eight-petalled lotus. I can't fix the diagram. The variant நான்றவிழ் (hanging loose) for நான்றவிம் may be the better reading.

729.reading: A hundred and sixty-six go round to the right, a hundred and sixty-six to the left, a hundred and sixty-six face each other, and a hundred and sixty-six enter.
729.nuance: நூறும் அறுபதும் ஆறும் may be one number (166) or three counts (a hundred, sixty, six). The subject is unnamed; breaths through the right and left channels, meeting and entering the central channel, is the likely sense in this chapter, but it is a guess.

730.reading: One who has mastered the left and right in Shakti's temple can hear music at midday; the sweet dance and Siva himself appear; we have spoken truth, by Sadananda's command.
730.nuance: Shakti's temple is taken as the body, and left and right (இடம் வலம்) as the left and right breaths (ida and pingala). The music (வாத்தியம்) is traditionally the inner nada heard in yoga, and கூத்து Siva's dance. The variant வாக்கியம் (speech) for வாத்தியம் would change what is heard.

731.reading: Bindu shining in its many forms as the letter ma, the letter sa recited in thought until it is attained, the mantra that turns back, and the abiding nada: when these are fully gained, they are the yogi's path of dharma.
731.nuance: மகாரம் and சகாரம் are letters of a mantra, traditionally of the five-syllable mantra, and are matched here with bindu and nada; their roles are not explained. மறிப்பது (that which turns back or blocks) and the last line's division (நாதம் அறப்பெற or நாத மறப்பு) are uncertain.

732.reading: Raising by contemplation the prana that stands straight with the whorl of the navel, fixing it first at the summit with Siva's mantra, and raising the apana by contemplation, one becomes Siva.
732.nuance: பிராணன் and அபானன் are the upward and downward vital airs; உந்திச் சுழி (the navel whorl) and முகடு (the summit, the crown) are their stations. சிவன் அவன் ஆமே, he becomes Siva, is the strongest claim in the chapter, and it rests on the technical practice.

733.reading: Mark the place two finger-breadths above the anus and below the linga; in this body the Lord too is there; see that this is the instruction that is not to be spoken.
733.nuance: The place is traditionally the muladhara, the base of the yogic body. ஆறா உடம்பு (the body that does not cool, or does not rest) is unclear. கூறா உபதேசம் can be 'instruction not to be told' (secret, from a guru) or 'instruction that cannot be told'.

734.reading: Those who closely embrace the blue-hued lady with fine jewels and hold to her as lasting will, as the world can see, lose their grey hair and wrinkles and become young again; by the supreme Nandi's command.
734.nuance: The plain reading is of union with a woman; the blue lady (நீல நிறனுடை நேரிழையாள்) is traditionally Shakti, or kundalini, and the embrace a yogic union. Both readings stand in the text. சதம் may mean 'lasting' or 'a hundred (years)'.

735.reading: If the cosmos contracts there is no ruin for it; if the body contracts the breath stays firm; if food is reduced there are many means; and one becomes the dark-throated Kapali.
735.nuance: அண்டம் and பிண்டம் are the cosmos and the body, the macrocosm and microcosm of yoga. 'Contracting' is unexplained: shrinking, withdrawal or restraint. The last line names Siva as Kapali (the skull-bearer with the dark throat); the yogi becoming him is the sense taken, though it could be the means being his.

736.reading: If one goes step by step through the cosmos to the back door set in the body, women with flower-decked hair that bees seek will look at it with desire: it becomes a fine body.
736.nuance: பிழக்கடை வாசல் (the back gate) is traditionally a passage of the yogic body, perhaps the rear channel up the spine; I can't fix it. The reward is outward beauty, desirable to women, which runs against the ascetic strain elsewhere in Tamil didactic verse.

737.reading: Before the torment of great, whirling Death rages, if you would see the anklet-bearing holy feet of the Lord who is in the burning blood and in the fire, there you can stand in the shade and in the clear.
737.nuance: அழலும் இரத்தம் and அங்கி (fire) are taken as the inner fire of the yogic body, where the Lord is seen. நிழலுளும் தெற்றுளும் is obscure: perhaps standing untouched in shade and in clear (light), or in any condition.

738.reading: The fire I saw, the four and seven kalas, the breath he saw with the whole body, and the awareness gained by seeing the flesh, taken as medicine: this is how the mango sapling stands and grows.
738.nuance: The list is compressed and its grammar uncertain. The mango sapling (மாங்கன்று) is an image of the body tended to grow, but how fire, kalas and breath make the medicine is not explained.

739.reading: If you take with love the Shakti of the arising Veda, with the straightness of rice as it grows, divide it into many crores of portions and be absorbed by the mantra that holds what is destined.
739.nuance: Nearly every phrase is obscure: சனவேத சத்தி (perhaps the Shakti of the arising Veda, perhaps a corrupt word), the rice image (the variant நீர்க்கொள நெல்லின், rice taking water, suggests growth fed by water), and ஊழ்கொண்ட மந்திரம். The reading is a guess at the words, not the sense.

links.note: On what the body is worth: the Naladiyar calls it a pot seeping filth from nine openings, attractive only through its skin, and the man who praises it a fool; Tirumular says he once held the body base (இழுக்கு) but found the Lord had made it his temple, and so cherishes it. The conflict holds if the Naladiyar's verse is read as a verdict on the body and not only as a remedy for lust.

Both value the body for what it yields, but the Naladiyar has the body thrown away like crushed cane once its juice is taken, while Tirumular says the body must be nurtured because life and true knowledge perish with it.

Both rest on the three humours of the medical writers, wind among them: the Kural says excess or lack of them brings disease, Tirumular names the time of day at which practice removes each, and promises the end of age as well.
The Kural says that eating in measure is how one who has a body keeps it long; Tirumular counts the reduction of food among the means of perfecting the body.
Both claim that Death can be overcome: the Kural by the power gained through austerity, Tirumular by seeing the Lord's feet in the inner fire before Death strikes.
